The crude transfers totaled an estimated 9 million barrels and were ultimately destined for Chinese independent refiners, commonly known as “teapots.” The activity has continued despite growing scrutiny of the large network of sanctioned and Iran-linked vessels operating in the region. The depletion of offshore storage comes even as oil exports from other Persian Gulf producers have recovered. If UANI’s estimate of roughly 10 million barrels remaining in Malaysian floating storage is accurate, the pool of crude available outside the blockade has fallen sharply. items.title: Panama Canal Expands Advance Transit Reservations for 2027 Dry Season
items.original_title: Panama Canal Expands Advance Transit Reservations for 2027 Dry Season
items.summary: The Panama Canal is expanding its long-term transit reservation program to the Panamax locks for the first time, giving more shipping customers the ability to secure passage months in advance during the 2027 dry season. The Panama Canal Authority said Monday that the next phase of its Long-term Slot Allocation, or LoTSA, program will cover transits from January 3 through April 3, 2027. The program will continue at the Neopanamax locks while a new pilot program introduces long-term slot allocations for vessels using the Panamax locks. The expansion comes as the Panama Canal continues adjusting its operating model following the severe drought that sharply restricted daily transits in 2023 and 2024 and exposed the vulnerability of the freshwater-dependent waterway to changing rainfall conditions. For carriers and vessel operators, the attraction of LoTSA is straightforward: guaranteed access to scarce transit capacity can make voyage planning more reliable, particularly during the dry season when water availability has historically placed the greatest pressure on Canal operations. By extending the program to the Panamax locks, the Canal is making that option available to a broader portion of the commercial fleet for the first time. The Panama Canal is easing restrictions on vessel draft and daily transits after improved rainfall and water-saving measures helped stabilize conditions in the waterway’s drought-sensitive watershed.

items.original_title: ‘More liberal’ India ends licence requirement for box ship reflagging
items.summary: As its emerging economy pursues maritime-driven growth, India appears willing to simplify the regulatory system for foreign-flag containerships operating out of the country. Reflecting a more liberalised approach, the Indian authorities have scrapped a licensing requirement for vessels chartered by foreign lines through local entities registered in the new business district in Gujarat State better known as “GIFT City”. Business units operating on the financial centre have multiple regulatory advantages – more particularly, significant tax exemptions – and several mainline and shortsea container lines reportedly already have presence at GIFT City, including CMA CGM, Maersk, and Unifeeder. And, acting on that strength, several container line heavyweights have implemented vessel reflagging in India – six changes by CMA CGM and twoby Maersk. While reflagging one vessel the Marseille-based carrier said: “With India playing an increasingly important role in the global trade, CMA CGM remains dedicated to supporting the country’s maritime ecosystem and contributing to its economic development through strategic initiatives and enhanced service offerings. The move to abolish a licensing requirement that involved considerable documentation for each call seeking to enter Indian waters is a significant policy relaxation, aimed at pushing the “ease-of-doing-business environment” for investors. And industry sources claimed it would allow “greater operational flexibility” for carriers.

items.summary: Renewed fighting in the Middle East has pushed gas markets back into crisis. US strikes on Iranian targets, Houthi advances on the Bab el-Mandeb strait and a shutdown of Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline have combined to send Brent above $100 per barrel and LNG prices racing toward $30 per MMBtu, erasing the price gap that once separated European and Asian buyers. The impact on supply is significant and growing. Rystad Energy now estimates conflict-related LNG production losses from Qatar at 64.8 Mtpa in 2026 and 22.9 Mtpa in 2027, a sharp increase from last month’s figures. In response, we have raised our 2026 price forecasts for TTF and Northeast Asian spot LNG by $1.0 per MMBtu, to $16.0 and $17.0 respectively, as low storage levels in Europe and uncertainty over winter arbitrage keep buyers on edge. The longer-term picture tells a different story. Supply and demand are expected to rebalance by 2028, and from 2029 the market is set to tip into oversupply, peaking at 81 Mtpa in 2032. For buyers and producers alike, the challenge is navigating a market that is tight today but loosening fast. Source: Rystad Energy

items.summary: China’s exclusion of soybeans from its planned tariff-reduction framework has left exporters optimistic that Beijing will increase purchases of other US farm and food products in the coming months to fulfill a commitment made earlier this year. China’s Ministry of Commerce said Sept. 28 that Beijing would consider reducing tariffs on a range of US agricultural and animal-protein products, including beef, pork, corn and wheat, but excluded soybeans. China purchased more than $10 billion in US farm and food products from January through July 2026, including $4.9 billion of soybeans and $5.2 billion of other agricultural commodities, according to US Census Bureau trade data. “Removal of the remaining 10% tariff that China has on US agricultural commodities could be key to boosting US competitiveness in the Chinese market,” S&P Global Energy CERA analysts said in a Sept. US beef and pork exports have historically accounted for a significant share of China’s purchases of US agricultural and food products, US traders said. During the tariff dispute in early 2025, China reduced its purchases of US pork and suspended US beef imports after Beijing stopped renewing export licenses for US meat-processing facilities in March 2025. China imposes a 13% duty on US soybeans, comprising a 3% most-favored-nation tariff and an additional 10% levy.

items.title: Korea pushes SMR ship lead as outdated rules spur global standards race
items.original_title: Korea pushes SMR ship lead as outdated rules spur global standards race
items.summary: As Korea’s shipbuilding industry accelerates development of vessels equipped with small modular reactors (SMRs), calls are growing for the creation of international rules. Existing nuclear safety regulations focus on land-based nuclear power plants, and maritime regulations focus on conventional ships, leaving a gap for “ships carrying reactors,” where standards to apply are not fully established. With the offshore SMR market preparing for commercial use, leading the formation of international standards and rules—no less than technology development—is seen as a factor that will determine future market competitiveness. For ships carrying next-generation SMRs to call at ports around the world, standards are needed that cover not only reactor safety but also maritime accidents such as collisions and groundings, port entry, and emergency response. International liability rules for damages in the event of an accident involving a nuclear-powered ship are also not functioning properly. IMO and International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) standards on port entry conditions were last revised in 1968. The Korea Atomic Energy Research Institute (KAERI) and Samsung Heavy Industries are developing a 174,000-cubic-meter LNG carrier based on a marine MSR, and HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering has designed a nuclear-powered container ship equipped with an SMR, winning approval in principle from DNV in Oct.

items.title: Europe’s diesel tightness persists into Q4
items.original_title: Europe’s diesel tightness persists into Q4
items.summary: Europe’s diesel/gasoil imports from outside the region hit the lowest September on record. Diesel/gasoil exports pointed to Europe from outside regions averaged only 1mbd in September, down 600kbd y-o-y. Russia and the Middle East account for most of the drop, together down 580kbd compared to last year. Diesel on the water pointed to Europe is more than 25% below last year’s levels, all points indicating that October will be another month of weak arrivals. Europe’s implied refinery runs fell by around 600kbd in September (according to our estimates), after reaching a year-to-date high in August. Strong margins have delayed maintenance at key refineries into 2027, including Tarragona (180kbd), Thessaloniki (66kbd) and Gonfreville (247kbd) (Argus), so maintenance season is likely to already have peaked in September this year, as opposed to the usual October. The US is still the key external supplier The US supplied 41% of Europe’s external diesel in September, at 400kbd, above year-ago levels but down from a dataset high of 445kbd in August. A growing portion of China’s diesel cargoes are moving on LR2s. Unless Asia’s diesel arb to Europe widens, China’s Q4 barrels will likely keep prioritising shorter-haul destinations amid high freight costs.

items.summary: Italian product tanker owner d’Amico International Shipping has exercised a $14m purchase option on the 2014-built MR tanker High Fidelity , paving the way for its entire operating fleet to return to full ownership. Operating arm d’Amico Tankers is expected to take ownership of the 50,000 dwt Hyundai Vinashin-built vessel around mid-January 2027, with the final price subject to a small adjustment depending on the actual transfer date. The ship is one of the last two vessels in d’Amico’s fleet still operating under bareboat arrangements. The company currently controls 28 product tankers on the water — 16 MRs, six handysizes and six LR1s — comprising 26 owned ships and two bareboat-chartered units. The move follows d’Amico’s decision in August to exercise a $15.3m option on sister-era MR High Discovery, which is due to return to full ownership in November. Once both transfers are completed, d’Amico will have no remaining bareboat-chartered ships. Both vessels were refinanced through sale-and-leaseback structures in 2022. At the time, d’Amico exercised previous options on High Discovery and High Fidelity for $20.3m and $19.2m respectively before refinancing them under new 10-year bareboat leases containing fresh purchase options. items.original_title: HD Hyundai delivers world’s first lashing-free containership
items.summary: HD Hyundai has delivered what it says is the world’s first containership designed to eliminate manual lashing, removing one of the most labour-intensive jobs in container shipping. The 13,000 teu vessel, which is methanol dual-fuelled, has been handed over toFrance’s CMA CGM after being built using HD Hyundai’s proprietary hybrid lashing-free system. HD Hyundai Heavy Industries developed and verified the core technology, while HD Hyundai Samho carried out detailed design and construction. HD Hyundai’s new arrangement does away with that work by extending cell guides above deck, allowing containers to be held in place without traditional lashing. The breakthrough centres on what HD Hyundai calls a portable bench, a standardised structure fitted between cell guides. The unit is the same size as a 40 ft container, meaning terminal cranes can handle it as part of normal cargo operations. HD Hyundai says the design boosts deck cargo capacity by more than 10% compared with similar existing ships while improving operational stability in heavy weather. The technology was presented to the IMO’s Sub-Committee on Carriage of Cargoes and Containers in 2024 and has since secured multiple patents. The Korean yard plans to expand the lashing-free technology to small and mid-sized vessels soon.

The new Long-term Slot Allocation, or LoTSA, phase will cover January 3 to April 3, 2027, with the established neopanamax system running alongside a new panamax pilot. For neopanamax vessels, 36 packages covering 270 slots will be offered, split between 165 northbound and 105 southbound passages. The panamax pilot will offer 51 packages and 288 slots, evenly spread at roughly three transits per day. The move builds on a system first introduced for the larger locks in 2024, when the Panama Canal Authority began offering blocks of future reservations to customers seeking greater scheduling certainty after the severe 2023-24 drought. Splash reported in May that neopanamax auction prices had surged to as much as $4m as Middle East disruption redirected more US energy cargoes through Panama. By August, one LPG carrier had paid a record $5.3m for priority passage as deteriorating water conditions and strong demand squeezed capacity. However, as MEG loadings continue to scale, recently boosted by the redirection of Saudi exports to the East, challenging STS capacity in the GoO, a diversification of the region’s trading patterns becomes increasingly inevitable. As RED III applies to all industries, there will also be competition from the airline and heavy transport industries in the use of bio-residues, and we suspect this will create additional risksin the maritime sector. Buyers in the sector may be exposed to lower-quality residues, for example, chemically variable feedstocks and/or blends from multiple residue streams. Pressure may mount on traceability systems, fraud risks may increase (due to misclassification of sustainabilityvalues in Proof of Compliance documents) and disputes over the chain of custodyaccumulate. Given the rising uptake of biofuels and the consequent risks, NorthStandard is recommending particular care in this area of marine fuel management.

items.summary: Taiwan’s U-Ming Marine Transport has committed up to $312m on six more bulkers in China, adding four ultramaxes and firming another pair of Newcastlemaxes as it presses ahead with plans to build a 100-ship fleet. Two separate Taiwan exchange disclosures from U-Ming’s Singapore subsidiary put the combined investment at between $296m and $312m. The larger ships are two 211,000 dwt newcastlemaxes at Jiangsu Hantong Ship Heavy Industry, priced at between $77m and $80m each for a total of $154m to $160m. U-Ming is also paying between $142m and $152m for four 64,000 dwt ultramaxes at Sumec Marine-controlled New Dayang Shipbuilding, equating to $35.5m to $38m per ship. The first of the ultramaxes is scheduled for delivery in the fourth quarter of 2029, with the remaining three following during 2030. The latest contracting advances an expansion plan approved by U-Ming earlier this year covering four 210,000 dwt bulkers and four ultramaxes. U-Ming has been steadily renewing and expanding its core dry bulk fleet while moving into new sectors. At its May investor presentation, the company was targeting a fleet of more than 100 vessels, with dry bulk remaining at the centre of the expansion. U-Ming said at the end of September that its owned, joint venture and newbuilding fleet had reached around 90 ships and passed the 10m dwt mark.

items.title: South Korea-Russia ocean volumes boosted by rail congestion in China
items.original_title: South Korea-Russia ocean volumes boosted by rail congestion in China
items.summary: Growing congestion along the Trans-China and Trans-Siberian railways, linking China and Russia, has boosted South Korea-Russia container volumes, encouraging shipping lines to consider deploying larger vessels this month. In August, more than 33,000 teu was transported from Busan to ports in Russia’s far east, such as Vladivostok, a slight increase on July. Of this, exports, excluding transhipment cargo, were 8,000 teu. Volumes are said to have remained at the same level in September, as South Korean shippers rushed to get cargo out before the country’s Thanksgiving Day holiday on 25-26 September and China’s week-long National Day on 1 October. Consequently, cargo “rollovers”, where shipments are delayed due to a lack of space, are becoming increasingly frequent and Busan-Vladivostok freight rates now average $1,700 per teu, up from $1,500 per teu in August, which had seen a $300 jump from July. A representative at Dong Young Shipping, which offers South Korea-Russia services, said: “We’re considering deploying larger vessels than those currently in use, so we can offer more slots.” Congestion around major Chinese hub ports following the East Asia typhoon season in August resulted in more Chinese shippers opting for rail freight to Europe. And as rail capacity has failed to keep pace with the surge in cargo volume, waiting times for train departures now exceed one week.

items.original_title: Empty box pile-up at port of Manila sparks truckers’ strike
items.summary: Customs brokers and hauliers are expected to voluntarily stop work today in advance of a three-day trucking strike in Manila, as a year-long standoff on carriers failing to remove their empties reaches its limit – Hapag-Lloyd having suspended bookings amid the chaos. Warning the protest could “last a week”, Reynaldo Soliman, chair of the Practicing Customs Brokers and Port Truckers Alliance, urged brokers not to secure gate passes, book trucks, or release shipments, until carriers reduced the number of empties at Manila. “Even though we want to ship, we cannot move,” Mr Soliman told local reporters, with the number of empties scattered around terminals, hauliers yards, and waiting on flatbeds to be removed, measured in the thousands with just 10% of volumes moving out of Manila’s ports. In a letter seen by The Loadstar , Bureau of Customs commissioner Ariel Nepomuceno told Port of Manila it needed to take measures to address the worsening empties backlog, suggesting boxes that had been waiting for more than 10 days be moved offsite. “Increasing yard utilisation levels at the Manila International Container Port and the port of Manila continue to adversely affect the efficient movement of cargo and the overall flow of port operations,” he wrote.

Its fleet renewal has also included the disposal of older supramax tonnage, including the 2008-built Anasa. items.title: South Africa’s port reform takes an important step forward
items.original_title: South Africa’s port reform takes an important step forward
items.summary: One battle doesn’t win a war, but just getting to a stage where South Africa’s port system can now be reformed is an achievement by itself. The decision of South Africa’s government to formally endorse the separation of Transnet National Port Authority (TNPA), the country’s de facto port landlord, from the Transnet rail operations is a step in the right direction – one that its shippers, forwarders, and other supply chain stakeholders have been demanding for years. Operations at South Africa’s key container gateways of Durban, Cape Town, Coega and Port Elizabeth have been plagued by congestion and delays for years. And while it’s great the government has finally kicked off the reform process of Transnet, it also means some of the really hard work begins now, as the South African Association of Freight Forwarders argues when it says the real imperative is “getting corporatisation right”. The central point of the reform is that TNPA will be moved out of the Transnet group – which will continue to manage Transnet Port Terminals, but with much reduced investment power – and become a standalone state organisation with the ability to take its own investment decisions on both infrastructure and superstructure, and independently manage landlord revenues.

items.original_title: Europe’s scrap demand set to surge as new EAFs loom: Eurofer
items.summary: Europe’s transition toward more electric steelmaking, with up to 20 electric arc furnaces expected to be commissioned in 2026-2030, adding 34 million-44 million metric tons of steel capacity, will increase the need for ferrous scrap, especially for high-quality material, the European Steel Association told Platts, part of S&P Global Energy. In 2025, the EU steel industry consumed 74.4 million mt of ferrous scrap. Its H1 2026 intake of 38.1 million mt has kept EU steel production and ferrous scrap utilization broadly in line with the first half of 2025, but Europe’s accelerating transition toward more electric steelmaking will trigger a surge in the EU’s steel scrap demand, according to Eurofer. This means Europe’s future steelmaking system will use a combination of scrap and primary iron units, rather than simply replacing today’s production with 100% scrap-based EAF output. But there won’t be a uniform European scrap-to-DRI ratio: mixes will be plant-specific with EAFs operating on a spectrum ranging from near-100% scrap to 50:50, or even DRI/hot briquetted iron-dominant blends, French said.

items.summary: Japan has imposed sanctions directly on individual vessels for the first time, targeting 35 ships linked to Russia’s shadow fleet as Tokyo steps up efforts to restrict Moscow’s oil-export network. Japanese companies will now need government permission to provide specified services to the 35 vessels and for capital transactions, including loans and debt guarantees, connected with their sale, purchase, lease or charter. Japan’s foreign ministry has identified all 35 ships by IMO number. It is the first time Tokyo has placed vessels themselves under sanctions, bringing Japan closer to the approach already adopted by the UK and European Union against ageing tankers moving Russian oil outside mainstream Western shipping, finance and insurance channels. The shipping measures formed part of a wider package that also froze the assets of 33 Russian organisations and nine individuals and introduced export restrictions against four entities in Turkey and the UAE. Tokyo said the vessel measures were aimed at ships being used to transport Russian crude and petroleum products while circumventing existing sanctions. items.original_title: Oil exports surge back through Hormuz despite mounting attacks
items.summary: Oil flows from the Middle East have climbed back above pre-war levels even as attacks on tankers around the Strait of Hormuz accelerate to their fastest pace since the conflict with Iran erupted on February 28. Provisional Kpler data shows regional crude exports exceeded pre-war volumes on four days during the final week of September, reaching between 19.5m and 22.5m barrels per day. The seven-day moving average stood at 18.5m barrels per day on October 1, compared with an average of around 18m barrels per day in the year before the war. The numbers cover Hormuz and Red Sea movements as well as terminal exports and ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman. Iraqi Oil Tankers Company has transported a 2m-barrel cargo through Hormuz on a chartered VLCC, taking responsibility for the crude beyond the strait rather than selling it on the traditional free-on-board basis at Basra. The surge in cargoes transiting Hormuz is being matched, however, by an equally sharp escalation in attacks. The 115,100 dwt Lipsi, operated by Greece’s Dynacom Tankers Management, was hit by an unknown projectile in Hormuz on Sunday, suffering engine-room damage. items.title: Where freight forwarders actually lose money
items.original_title: Where freight forwarders actually lose money
items.summary: More often than not, a forwarder closes a clean month and still watches the margins come in light. Most forwarders already know where it went: into the charges that were never recovered and the costs that were never meant to happen. A demurrage charge that was never passed on to the customer. Forwarders already have more data than they can read. Everything after is just a record of money already gone. So, the job is narrower than what most tech pitches: flag the handful of shipments where an unexpected charge is about to be incurred, whether that is demurrage building, a customs delay, port congestion that holds up haulage, or a misinterpreted contract, and put them in front of the operator early enough for them to act. Command Center surfaces the risks, the AI agents take routine tracking and reconciling off the operator’s plate, and Freight Audit checks carrier invoices against the contract and the actual shipment, so overcharges and miscalculated D&D are caught before they are paid rather than written off after. BCOs are already benchmarking their forwarders on exactly that, and it is often the difference between an account that renews and one that goes out to tender. For most forwarders, the honest answer is uncomfortable, and it is also the easiest money they will find all year.

items.title: What Is the Shadow Fleet, and Why Is It So Hard to Count?
items.original_title: What Is the Shadow Fleet, and Why Is It So Hard to Count?
items.summary: There Is No Official Shadow Fleet List The shadow fleet, also called the dark fleet, refers to tankers and support vessels that rely on deceptive shipping practices to move sanctioned or high-risk commodities while concealing their true origin, ownership, or destination. It has no standing in law, and that is where the difficulty starts. Why Every Published Estimate Is Different Ask five organizations how large the shadow fleet is, and you will get five answers, sometimes differing by a factor of three. The useful question is narrower: Does this vessel exhibit the behavior, and what is my exposure if it does? A vessel flying a legitimate flag has the right of innocent passage through the territorial sea, and on the high seas it is subject to the jurisdiction of its flag state. There is a lag between a vessel starting to operate as part of the shadow fleet and that vessel appearing on a sanctions list. During that gap, the vessel is detectable through its behavior and invisible to a list check. Vessels without a valid flag are stateless, and under Article 110 of UNCLOS, a warship may board a ship on the high seas where there are reasonable grounds to suspect it is.

items.title: Strait of Hormuz security, decarbonisation among key issues discussed by BIMCO committees
items.original_title: Strait of Hormuz security, decarbonisation among key issues discussed by BIMCO committees
items.summary: The security situation in the Strait of Hormuz and the Black and Red Seas, as well as environmental topics, were among the key issues discussed when BIMCO’s Maritime Safety & Security Committee (MSSC) and Marine Environment Committee (MEC) met on 30 September and 1 October. Members considered the implications of regional conflicts, attacks on shipping, drones, mines and navigational disruption. The committees also discussed a broad range of other regulatory, safety and environmental issues affecting the day-to-day operation of ships. Our committees bring together industry expertise to identify practical challenges and help shape BIMCO’s positions in discussions with the IMO, governments and regulators. Digitalisation was another major theme, including the opportunities it offers for efficiency, compliance and safety, as well as the growing importance of cyber security and supporting seafarers as technology develops. Members also discussed the safe adoption of alternative fuels, including ammonia, hydrogen and methanol, and future safety frameworks for advanced modular nuclear reactors. The proposed legally-binding international convention on biofouling was also discussed, with an emphasis on ensuring that future requirements are practical, science-based and capable of consistent implementation across the global fleet. Other topics included search and rescue and mixed migration, underwater radiated noise, marine plastics and plastic pellet transportation, and implementation of the Hong Kong Convention on ship recycling. Source: BIMCO, https://www.bimco.org/news-insights/bimco-news/2026/10/01-mec-mssc/

items.title: Clean tanker markets size up impact of potential US diesel export curbs
items.original_title: Clean tanker markets size up impact of potential US diesel export curbs
items.summary: US restrictions on diesel exports would upend Atlantic Basin clean tanker demand at a moment when the global middle-distillate market is reeling from simultaneous supply shocks in Russia and the Middle East, BRS Shipbrokers said in a report. The impact on medium-range tanker earnings in particular could be swift and severe, BRS said Sept. 28. US President Donald Trump had floated a diesel export ban in response to record domestic fuel prices ahead of midterm elections. Tanker implications A full ban could strand around 1.35 million b/d of US Gulf diesel exports — the equivalent of four MR2-sized cargoes per day — with Europe and Latin America most exposed given the absence of readily available alternative supply, BRS said. Pressure would fall most heavily on MR2s, which carry more than 90% of US diesel exports, BRS said. There could also be bleed-in to MR1 markets as MR2s compete for smaller stems, while clean tankers would likely ballast away from the US Gulf, putting pressure on tonnage lists elsewhere, BRS said. The offsetting factor for the broader clean tanker complex is a potential redirection of Asian barrels westward. “With the potential diesel ban coming, the appetite for US diesel exports is declining because these products are needed at home, whether there’s a ban or not,” Simpson said.
